paragraphs.text: THE COMMONITORIUM OF ORIENTIUS.
BOOK ONE.
Whoever you are who, hastening toward the rewards of eternal life,
desire what will last forever rather than what will perish,
learn the way that opens heaven and puts death to flight, that avoids rough ground
and runs along a blessed path.
For we, overcome both by the vices of the flesh and by time,
tread our earthly road [?] without grief:
and this alone is now our joy, amid our mingled hopes:
that what we do not do, others at least may do,
so that—since we now spend this life, which flees away at once,
caught by faithless allurements,
wanton, wretched, deceitful, brief, fickle, vain,
alas, the evil source of our offenses hurls us headlong [?]—
you may leave behind all these things that will swiftly die,
and with steadfast faith hold fast to what will not die.
So come, lend attentive ears and an unoccupied mind:
life is what I must teach, life is what you must seek.
But so that the teaching of our little book may be the better,
and the course of the poem may keep to right paths,
I resolve to entreat you, almighty God, with heart and voice,
and not to loosen my tongue without you, O Christ,
you who in your kindness are wont to take darkness from the blind by restoring light,
to put hearing into deaf ears,
to drive out the cruel diseases of body and mind,
and to loosen the mouths of the mute:
in your keeping lies the work of our heart and of our mouth:
grant me to understand, grant me to be able to speak,
so that your gifts may quicken our tongue,
and through you, about you, our speech may be pleasing to you,
since at your command a she-ass, surpassing all
nature, spoke with our human voice,
and the beast terrified Balaam, as he goaded its back,
with its wondrous speech—
Balaam, who, at the great and repeated entreaty of a frightened king,
was preparing dire words against the holy people,
yet could not make his own tongue, once set moving, obey him,
saying one thing with his mouth and desiring another in his heart.
For, about to curse, he began to bless abundantly,
spending on one purpose lips prepared for another.
Therefore, unless you, Christ, supply eloquence, unless you supply understanding,
and unless you, Christ, guide the strivings of the soul,
all men will have mouths both mute and dull,
and even what they are able to do, they will not be able to do.
First of all, you must recognize that there is a twofold life,
granted to man by the Lord for good reason,
so that, since the body is a brute thing of earthly weight,
while the soul is quickened by the breath of God,
the soul's existence should suffer no loss through ending,
while life in this fragile body should be brief.
The one, the law of birth brings to everyone first;
the other is gained by diligence and by one's own merits.
To be born is not in our power, nor to live long;
but this life can prepare the life that follows.
And though we receive both at the Lord's will,
and neither befalls us unless God commands it,
yet the first is swept downhill in a swift whirl,
while the one that follows is given for all time.
Into the first we come unknowing, by no merit of ours;
the second comes to us won by the utmost toil.
We are born so that we may seek the Lord of heaven, earth, and sea
with wakeful and wholehearted zeal.
We seek him so that who he is, how great, of what kind, and what he does,
we may come to know with true judgment.
We come to know him so that, having found him, we may worship him with fitting praise;
we worship him so that he may grant us everlasting life.
And we worship not by offering incense, not by shedding blood,
not drenched with wine, not heavy with feasting.
Gold, clothing, perfume, cattle, libations, gems,
and whatever men think rare or precious,
lie before God like worthless lumps of earthly matter,
like mud, like filth, just so without honor.
All things belong to him to whom we confess that we belong.
Nothing is our own: he possesses it, he gave it.
For see, he proclaims through the holy mouth of the prophet:
“I do not want your goats, I do not want your calves.
The beauty of the field is mine, and the glory of heaven:
for the world is mine, and what is in the world is mine.
Let the vows you owe be paid to me from a holy heart;
let the sacrifice of praise and a pure voice honor me.”
Therefore, our reader, you can plead nothing
in these admonitions that is difficult for you.
It is not set far off, it need not be sought elsewhere;
there is no need of property, of expense, of price.
It is enough that the Lord of the world and Father of all things,
in whose power lie both good and evil,
who in his greatness surpasses whatever words a speaker can say,
one, incorporeal, and holy forever,
embracing all things and ever one in all,
you should devoutly believe in your heart and, believing, entreat with your mouth.
But why do I use only bare words of my own like this,
as if there were no admonitions of God on this matter?
For remember that it was first enjoined under the old law,
which was long ago written on tablets of stone,
and is now renewed by the grace given through Christ the Lord,
as the venerable voice of the Gospel sounds it forth,
so that what stone once held, our hearts might now hold,
and faith, twice repeated, might be the richer:
“With all your affection and with all your inmost being,
and with all your heart, love the Lord your God.”
And rightly so: for what could you ever more justly render,
bound as you are by such great gifts?
It was he who, when you lay as clay in the dregs of earth,
took from you the lot of being mud forever;
he who—that you consist of limbs, that you are guided by a mind,
that you speak with a tongue, that you are wise with reason,
that you touch with hands, walk with feet, perceive with eyes,
hear with ears, smell with nostrils, taste with mouth—
grants you all this of his own goodness before any merit,
being at once father and lord of body and soul;
and not content with this one gift alone, by which
he furnished you with limbs and refined you with senses,
he who gave you life also bestows life's comforts,
so that it may be endowed for you with every delight.
See, for you the sky hangs aloft, for you the land draws back from the sea,
the air is held in balance, the ocean surges;
nights and days follow one another through the months of the year;
the sun shines, the stars gleam, the moon glows red.
Spring pours out charming flowers amid varied buds,
summer ripens fields now heavy with crops,
autumn is drenched with new wine, the olive rich with oil,
and winter, with fires drawn near, knows nothing of cold.
You strengthen overhanging roofs to keep off the rains;
you know nothing of the winds, with houses set against them;
and, combing the shaggy back of the woolly sheep,
you cover your chilled limbs in soft wrappings;
nor are smooth garments of snow-white linen lacking;
there are cloaks too of Eastern fleece:
the one the fruitful earth will give back to you once the seed is sown,
the other the Seres gather from tall trees.
In short, whatever you have through the whole year as it rolls round,
all of it the care of God gives you.
The plain grows green with harvest, the hillside is clothed with vines,
from various trees you reap mellow fruit,
and, providently spending your effort on a fertile garden,
you take useful vegetables whenever you please.
You kindle the resinous pine for light wherever you wish,
and a waxen flame glitters on noble tables.
Nor is the earth, made subject to man, bidden to serve him
only with earthly things, through their various uses:
even whatever moves near the clouds, whatever
rolls hidden away in the deep sea,
now with deceiving bait, now with linen woven into nets,
you seek out from here or there by countless skills.
Now fish are drawn up for you from the lowest depths,
now birds are tricked in the highest air.
Dense herds of wild beasts fall before the hunter,
struck from afar by javelins or entangled in nets.
You strike down what lies before you with iron, you halt with dogs what flees,
you curb the mouth of the fierce horse with bridles.
You drive oxen to the curved yoke, goats to the milking pail;
sweet honey drips for you from wrinkled combs.
You bring forth gems from rocks and gold from sands,
and smelt pliant metals from the earth with fire;
you distinguish the herbs that heal grim diseases,
diligently driving off deadly sickness by your skill.
Moreover, so that you may take goods from a foreign shore,
and give your own to others and seek what belongs to others,
you will run the rivers with oars and the seas with sail:
you will travel distant ways without toil.
Or if you fear the sea, you will set carriages rolling,
and the land will spread itself out to be marked by your wheels.
Then, if your travel-tossed body seeks pleasant rest,
warm baths will receive you, dusty as you are;
and, stripped of all your clothing in the hollow bath,
you will soothe your weary limbs in tamed waters.
With so many and such great goods won for you by the Lord's gift,
what worthy return, then, do you make with devoted love?
Or with what wealth, with what gifts can you repay these things,
or with how much service can you pay for them?
Yet the Lord, to whom all things belong, does not ask for these:
it is enough that you, a beloved servant, love your Lord.
Next follows the form of the second commandment as well:
that your neighbor be to you just as you are to yourself.
I recognize here a saving law of lasting benefit,
which by a single duty provides for all.
For when the care of another is entrusted to me, it follows
that the care of me is likewise entrusted to another.
See how beast leads beast to fertile pastures,
how the glad heifer lows to her own herd.
They answer with a murmur, they speak with what voice they can,
and a gentle tongue is wont to lick each in turn.
Nor are the creatures that the sea hides beneath its waves without affection,
and bird is gentle to bird and beast to beast.
Then, if ever a robber comes out of any band,
the stronger pressing the weak with claw or jaw,
whether the matter concerns birds or wild beasts,
they strive, with help gathered from every side,
by running, by flocking, by cry, by flight, to rescue their captured companion—
they want to, even if they cannot.
And since by the gift of nature alone they so protect one another,
though they have no strength of counsel or of reason,
what wonder if mutual care binds man to man
when he follows the Lord's awesome commands,
and one skilled in experience, wit, resources, and reason
should, as a brother, look after your interests as his own?
Hence comes that rightly pleasing maxim, which binds
the human race together on equal terms:
“Do not do to others whatever you do not want done to you,
and do to others what you want done to you.”
What race of men is there, what rite, what sex or age
that would deny this is right, that would deny this is easy?
What does this compact commandment not embrace in its breadth?
What could be handed down more fully than in this brevity?
For just as I would not want what is evil done to me,
so in turn I would want what is good done to me.
No informer is needed, no teacher is sought:
we know from ourselves what is good and what is evil.
You will surely rejoice if, as you travel by night, someone
kindly leads you to a nearby lodging:
you too, then, be attentive, provide a roof and take in
whoever is a traveler late at night.
When naked, you wish to be covered with clothing; when thirsty, to be called to drink;
when hungry, you wish to be filled with food:
let a concern equal to that for your own hardship move you too:
share cloaks, cups, and food with the wretched.
See, when you fall you ask for a hand; when sad, for comfort;
when afraid, for help; when in doubt, for counsel:
offer these to the sad, the doubtful, the fearful, the falling:
in a like case, love, so that you may be loved.
Surely you do not want to be accused on a false charge:
then be afraid to accuse others on a false charge.
You hate a thief: shun theft. You do not want to lose
what is yours by force: do nothing violently.
You do not want agreements made with you to waver in uncertain keeping:
then keep your promised word with a steady heart.
You would like to cut out the tongue that slandered you:
take care that no spiteful words of yours brand anyone.
When you ask for a loan, you want to receive the money at once:
then let a ready right hand help the one who asks you for a loan.
You condemn those puffed up with pride: lay aside your own swelling;
what you shun in the lofty, let those beneath you never meet in you.
Surely, if you have a sister, or a mother, or a dear wife,
whose lives you would not have stained by grievous rumor,
you take care, with watchful devotion, for their lasting chastity,
as son, or brother, or husband:
if an adulterer should assail these names you revere,
you think the sword not enough for vengeance.
Are you not guilty under the same penalty if you too secretly
set about tempting chaste marriage beds?
Hence it was that the Lord commanded under the first law
that crimes be weighed against equal punishments:
loss for loss, wound for wound, a tooth
paid for a tooth taken, eyes for eyes.
Likewise, so that the reckless man who sought to take another's life
should give up his own before the judge,
and the guilty could not call the judgment unjust,
vengeance was decreed for wicked crimes.
And though the grace of Christ has changed this for the better,
teaching gentleness rather than violence,
yet whatever the one law or the other commands is right,
whether you repay at once or act with patience.
Yet he is the better man who rejoices in Christ as his avenger,
if he leaves to the Lord what the Lord has claimed for himself.
Therefore, by devout prayers and holy deeds, bring it about
that both this present life and the life to come may approve you,
so that you, whom uprightness commends in this swiftly fleeing life,
may be received after death by everlasting glory.
For, assured by our admonitions, remember that all things will endure
which fools now think will perish:
and believe that souls, with the same limbs returning,
will take back the very covering of the body.
Faces, color, blood, veins, skin, bones, hair—
just as they now waste away, so they will come again,
not only those that well-built stone tombs preserve,
or that Arabian powder and perfume cover and keep firm:
but quicker than a word, to be formed into limbs, there will return
a portion from the tombs, a portion from the rivers.
What the wind has wasted with its blast, what a beast with its bite,
what flame has burned up, and what a falling ruin crushes,
all will be present, all will come together from every quarter,
part torn by bird or fish, part by wild beasts;
and what long age now slowly dissolves,
the Lord's trumpet will restore in an instant.
So, according to the deserts of their deeds, in the same body
in which they did either good or evil—
the flesh, that is, returning to obey the motions of the souls—
punishment will receive the guilty, and glory the just.
But why should you doubt, when what goes before shows
that your faith in what is to come should be plain?
Look at the woods stripped bare by winter's cold
now growing lush again with foliage once despaired of.
The vine that stood mourning, its shoots cut away,
is clothed with leaves and arrayed with fruit.
The stalk of grain turns golden with dense ears,
from a grain that only lately lay rotting in the earth,
and the fields that were lately rough with gloomy sloth
smile gladly with new shoots and blush with flowers.
The year itself, enclosed by its varied months,
bears the likeness of death as its seasons change,
when spring is driven off by autumn and cold by heat,
and, as with human affairs, one thing comes and another goes.
Yet by this everlasting custom, as long as God allows,
it turns round, each season taking its office in turn;
and while the moving wheel of the long year follows itself round,
it is born and dies, falls and returns.
For our end does not meet an end, and the death
by which we first die is itself dead forever.
With motion that will ever live and sensation that remains,
every human being will live for all time.
Man will live: but here weeping follows my words;
for I think man's lot would have been better thus:
along with the feeling of life to lay aside the feeling of punishment,
and, once born, to become like the unborn,
than now, with sins holding sway throughout his life,
to be dead to life and alive to torments.
For I beg you not to believe, to cut short that dreadful punishment,
that the deserved flame swiftly devours the guilty [?].
Look at the hills sunk in everlasting fires,
burning without ceasing, yet not diminished:
and see how cool springs and blue rivers
are always pouring out water, yet always have it.
So the avenging fire will forever ravage the wretched,
so as forever to keep rich fodder for itself.
If you think these things false, you will rightly find them true hereafter:
but you will escape them as false, if only you now fear them as true.
Therefore, if everlasting life follows after death,
gladdening the just and tormenting the guilty,
strive with all your strength and all your prayers
to keep on the ways that lead aright.
Trample underfoot the world, together with the prince of death,
and flee from trusting in wanton pleasures.
Above all, always scorn faces renowned for beauty,
and take the power of judging away from your eyes.
No one will carry glowing fire and leave his clothes untouched;
no one among trumpets will fail to catch the sound with his ear.
No one among flowers, surrounded by charming scents,
will fail to pluck with his fingernail the rose that is always at his nostrils.
No one long thirsty and scorched by much sun
will bend over cool waters and not drink of them.
No one making his way on foot in wintertime
will escape being sprinkled with rain and soaked.
No one, though inside the walls, in time of war
lives either wholly secure or wholly safe.
Meeting offers sight; soon the eyes, from seeing,
conceive flames and give birth to sin.
Just as when a fisherman's hook is cast with guile,
the soul is first caught, and afterward dies as well.
First stain of evil—alas, woman! The serpent's guile drove you,
and through you drove man, away from the Lord.
You were the cause of the good that was snatched away, you the door of death,
you so quickly deceived, you so quickly deceiving.
Come then, you who strive that your heart be stained by no blemish,
and to be pure with a pure mind:
as you flee from snares, fire, swords, and sharp poisons,
so flee from looking on a much-praised face.
I will not now recount, through so many ages, how many
peoples women's faces have ruined.
I pass over the disasters of Sparta, the wars of Troy,
and how near, Rome, your downfall came through a rape,
when nations under no law of the Lord, nor tamed
to the right way of life by any admonitions of the saints,
went wherever frenzy drove them and wanton lust led them,
and whatever pleased them was also lawful.
From the sacred books, I say, from the sacred books learn
into what great disgrace shameful love has led.
Dinah's beauty, Shechem, destroyed you as you rushed on in excessive love,
together with your father and your city.
For the brothers' devoted care for their wrongly violated sister
promised her in marriage and avenged her with the sword.
David too, praised in the song of the psalms,
was brought down from his lofty throne by a pleasing form,
when, his crime discovered, he covered his wickedly wanton body
with sackcloth and ground it down with ashes.
Tamar's beauty drove two brothers at the same time
into the crimes of incest and of the sword.
One defiles her, the other avenges her defilement:
a vengeance that is just ceases to be dutiful.
Even Solomon himself, whose wisdom in ancient
times was renowned throughout the whole world,
is led into sin, ensnared by forbidden love,
bowing his shameful neck to a woman's yoke;
and, once he forgot the Lord, the proclamations of praise
that had adorned him as a young man rightly forsook him as an old one.
A form that pleased the king handed you over to death, Haman;
a form carried off your head, General Holofernes.
Samson, famous for his wondrous strength,
was handed over by a comely form to the cruel Philistines.
That holy man, a soldier victorious in so many battles until then,
is, alas, wickedly subdued by the wiles of a company of women,
so that now, defiled—since crimes give birth to punishment—
he gave his kisses to maidens and his back to swords.
You too, so dearly loved by the Levite though not his wife,
handed over by night to the young men's frenzied lust,
through zeal for vengeance drove whole tribes into war,
content either to destroy or to perish,
so that, your limbs scattered in a mangled funeral, Gibeah
was made a pyre, burned with dreadful fires.
Not even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths
could I set out how much harm a pleasing form does.
The blessed apostle cries out to a wanton world,
laying down strict rules even for lawful marriage beds:
the man bound to a wife and the man free because he has spurned a wife
do not stand on the same footing in religion.
Care for his wife keeps the husband entangled;
the unmarried man wishes to have won God alone.
But since the eyes sometimes give way, and all that is upright
slips at a perilous fork in the road,
if the impious enemy sets out to stain your pure mind,
ever exulting to tempt chaste faith,
take up the weapons with which to guard the holy walls of your heart:
let the cross be your shield, let the cross be your sword.
With suppliant tears, with groaning, prayer, and beating of the breast,
seek the God who saves, night and day.
And lest hope little by little coax along an easy love,
keep drawing back your slipping foot from the precipice.
For I try to help the wretched not as one who does not know,
having suffered all the things I tell you to flee.
Do you look at beauty? Look rather at the cruel punishments,
look at what you praise, look at what you should fear,
and with inner eyes and true light see
from earth to heaven and from man to the Lord.
Here pleasure is brief, soon to be shut by a narrow end;
there is a devouring flame with everlasting sulfur.
Hear the prophet crying out with a lofty voice,
whether you read the old commandments or the new:
“What praise is there in a face? Believe that all flesh is grass,
for the glory of the flesh will be like the flower of grass.”
For just as a stroke cuts down flowers, heat wears them away,
rains beat them down, and a stronger wind snatches them off,
so whatever face pleases, time can consume it,
and swelling and bruising can despoil it.
And to say nothing of death itself, which crushes all things,
how much power do diseases, fevers, and ulcers have?
These hairs that now are white with dingy gray
once did not fear comparison with pitch.
Faces that now sag mournfully with ugly wrinkles
once displayed a vain beauty for all to gaze upon.
The foot that now totters, trembling in slack skin,
once scarcely left a mark on the ground it lightly trod.
Neck, throat, hands, and what now makes everyone shudder
were once, alas, a cause of madness to the wretched.
Eyes, which a moist rheum now bathes in ugliness,
once shone like the glowing torches of the stars.
Consider: what blooms for a few years does not last,
and yet the guilt remains to be wept for everlastingly.
Therefore you will scorn girlish faces and comely forms
with your head either turned aside or bowed down.
And so that you may be thoroughly pure in heart as in body,
so as to bring no one under suspicion of guilt,
take pains with care and always providently aim
that no woman be too closely joined to you.
The wind will lose its strength if nothing stands in its way;
if fuel is lacking, fire will be in vain.
And lest one sex alone be thought
urged by these commands toward the right paths of life,
whatever men learn, let a woman believe is said to her:
this sex too has both its merit and its punishments.
Let her hate to look boldly at unknown faces,
and let her hide herself even from familiar eyes.
For eyes that play with a wickedly mingled smile
often speak alluringly while the mouth is silent.
And love, like the tears that injury forces to flow,
rises from the eyes and makes its way to the depths of the heart.
Therefore, by the same law of precept by which young men are warned,
let a chaste woman flee from all men.
If now with a chaste body you have trampled on the body's
allurements, shake off the burden that remains in your heart.
For there is wont to creep in, from the gall of black poison,
envy, mother of manifold crime.
Unhappy envy, itself destined to die, prepared death:
through it an angel fell from the citadel of lofty heaven,
and while he hastens to drive man from the heavenly kingdom,
he himself first deserved to be thrust down into darkness.
From this came the Lord's avenging sentence upon all;
this one vice is answerable for all the other deaths:
this is the rage of war, this the discord that breaks peace,
harming itself more than the one it cruelly wishes to harm.
This, through the great crime of his brothers, was for Joseph
the cause first of slavery, and then of rule.
This stained Cain with the blood of his righteous brother;
this very nearly caused David's death,
when, the war now won by his strength alone,
his father-in-law would not have his son-in-law exalted with praise.
Driven by this, the laborer of the first hour, groaning,
strives to get the better of the digger of the eleventh.
This at last gave Christ up to the mockery of the cross,
while spite did the work that belief should have done,
and the headlong people saw the signs and miracles
with their eyes, but did not take them into their hearts.
To such a degree had wicked envy, with frenzied zeal,
turned them all from the truth to crime,
that it was not that they did not know, but that they would not believe, that then
man was to be glorified through the Lord.
Remember, next, to shun with no lighter care
the single vice of avarice, which holds countless crimes.
In all the lands the sun beholds and the seas enclose,
those the days visit and those the darkness covers,
whatever spreads across a world unknown to us,
in all kingdoms, among all peoples,
in the minds of the many infected with this disease, this is
the root, the cause, the head, the fount, and the origin of evil.
Whatever the Lord had formed for harmless uses,
this has ruined by wickedly perverting its purpose.
Why do you complain of cruel harbours and raging winds,
of grim seas notorious for shipwrecks?
Take the oak felled in the woods, its timber old with years,
and if it is no use for beams, put it on the fire.
Be content with your own, and if anything grows in some far-off corner of the world,
patiently accept that it was denied to you.
Then you will watch the heaving of the sea and the blasts of savage storms
without a care from the safety of the shore.
You greedy men have turned the uses of nature into vice,
so that things born good become evil through depraved use.
Iron, born from the earth to serve the earth,
curved in the sickle and rigid in the ploughshare,
we arm for slaughter and dreadful deaths, the crimes of war,
with pikes, missiles and swords.
We received fire to drive off the fierce cold,
to drive off the darkness and to cook our meals;
in our madness we began to hurl flames onto houses
and to set them under bodies to burn them,
as though robbery were too small a crime
unless the robber carried off wealth spattered with blood,
and unless extreme violence forced the wretched, with all kinds of torture,
after losing what they have, to reveal whatever is hidden.
Greed has made brothers hateful to brothers, and has made parents' lives
hateful to their children.
To make false out of true and true out of false
is what this savage vice teaches through countless snares.
At its prompting Ananias, guilty of holding back part of the gold,
passed wholly into death,
and not alone: for an equal punishment joined to the wretched man
his partner in the crime of foul deceit.
It is greed that has left wretched men, at the hour of death,
unable to trust safely in their last wills.
Documents are swapped, a witness is hunted up from anywhere,
who speaks falsehood with his lips and suppresses the truth in his heart.
Look-alike seals are engraved; a wicked hand learns,
alas, to imitate falsely counterfeited handwriting,
so that a man is believed to have become father of another's child, and a son
cannot be the heir of his own father.
Under its leadership the adulterer passes untroubled among the guards
and by bribes reaches the chaste bedchamber.
Men rush into every wickedness with minds and hands ready,
if you set gold as the price of the crime.
Tell me, I ask, wretched man, why such madness slackens [?] the reins,
so that what is already enough for you is not enough?
Do you hurry to join lands to boundless lands,
you who must be shut up in the marble of a little sarcophagus?
Do you strive to grow richer by another's loss?
What you seize from others will soon belong to someone else.
And all too quickly you will grieve over your losses,
just as those grieved who held it before you.
Do you build vast towers as though they will never fall,
when you yourself are going to die so swiftly?
For your sleep a polished chamber is adorned, gleaming with thin glass
and with marbles of many colours,
as if safe repose would not come under a roof of joined timbers
to a heart that is truly at peace.
Surely water rinses a thirsty mouth no differently
whether the palms of the hands offer it or a hollowed gem;
and the hunger of a ravenous belly will take in just the same
the food a crystal dish provides and the food a plain plate provides.
Does not the shaggy sheep give you a cloak
better for driving off the icy cold of winter
than a garment which, weighed down with metal drawn out into slippery threads,
hampers each step you take?
What use to you is a see-through garment, which with its flimsy covering
displays to strangers' eyes limbs that ought to be covered?
Silver, heaps of gold and the flashing gem
come from the world and belong to the world: from here they come, and here they stay.
You came into life naked, and naked you will return;
you brought nothing with you, and you can take nothing away.
Yet you can take the world's gifts with you if you scorn them here:
send your wealth on ahead to be doubled, since you are going to follow it.
For the goods you hoard too closely will soon not be yours;
if you do not keep them for yourself, then they will be yours.
Gifts given by a dying man are no gifts at all,
for he gives what is already ceasing to be his.
The one who, healthy and fearing nothing, with a calm mind,
has deprived himself while still alive—he is the one who has given.
And what he took from himself will be restored to him in better form:
whoever gives what would perish will soon receive what is whole.
For what is stored in heaven no thief, no enemy will carry off,
no moth or rain or devouring flame will consume;
and you will store in heaven whatever you give to the poor
for the name of Christ, with your eyes on Christ.
For after the mystery of the flesh he took on, he says:
"I am clothed in the naked, relieved in the wretched,
visited in prisoners, cared for and comforted in the sick,
helped in the little ones, protected in widows;
and whatever you do or fail to do for someone in misery,
believe me, is done to me or not done to me."
And so that, being poor, you cannot plead poverty
as a cover for unjust greed:
if you lack the means a needy man asks for,
if you have no food or warm water to refresh him,
when a thirsty man asks, a cup of cold water offered
in the name of Christ can win a reward.
Comfort the wretched beggar in whatever way you can,
and if you have no gifts, you will give prayers.
For in God's sight the will itself will not be lost,
which, though it cannot do good, at least desires it.
This is why the Lord, by his blessed teaching, willed
that all people be joined together by the love of peace,
and what he had previously commended through the holy prophets
he handed on to his disciples with his own lips,
since the love of peace, kept in a pure heart, can do nothing unjust, nothing harsh, nothing violent,
nothing frivolous, nothing greedy, nothing oppressive, nothing fickle,
either in its deeds or in the words it speaks.
Such is the love of peace preserved in a chaste heart.
Hence the harmony of peace holds the whole world together,
a harmony given by reason's design even to creatures without reason.
And though cold things fight with fiery ones, soft with hard,
moist with dry, slow with swift,
through hidden causes and by silent governance
it unites the whole of creation in a single covenant of peace.
So too, if you will allow great things to be compared with small,
the love of peace restrains the people of this bodily world,
so that, united under an earthly ruler, they learn
to offer their prayers together to the King of heaven.
Therefore, sinner like me—or rather, lesser than me,
for I surpass everyone in my crimes—
love peace when you are appeased, and love peace when you are wronged;
let there be peace in your heart, and peace on your lips.
Drive out hatred, scorn threats, put away pride;
let no length of time keep hold of your grievance,
so that the sun, as it sets, may leave you keeping the bonds of gentle peace,
and as it returns, may find you keeping them still.
BOOK TWO.

If you walk by my counsel, most faithful reader,
you tread safely on the dark-blue neck of the serpent.
And when Christ comes as judge, you will soon go out to meet him,
carried through the yielding air on gentle winds,
provided that at no time does any part
of these commandments slip from your care.
But if the glory of a windy tongue should move you,
the glory Cicero urges with his empty eloquence;
if instead jesting, banquets, idle talk and pleasure must be shunned,
so that you must part even from those of your own age,
with what zeal will you keep the words of my little book,
so as to be joined to God by the merits of your life?
The chief labour is to despise flattering praise,
which in its ambition drags men headlong,
and always hastens with silent motion to the inmost parts,
and sits, a bitter plague, in the very vitals.
Since we want whatever we do to be approved,
and want everyone to look kindly on our vices,
the miser calls himself thrifty, giving it a softer name,
and cruelty is veiled under the name of sternness;
with all our zeal and all our art we strive
that whatever we say or do may please.
But you, if you wish to be approved by Christ alone,
seek no glory at all from men.
For when you are cast down, you will soon be exalted,
and being small for the Lord's sake, you will be great with the Lord.
Whatever wrong may trouble you, bear it with patience;
and if you have suffered evil, repay no one evil in kind.
See, Christ prays to the Father for those who tear him;
Stephen too entreats, and James too entreats,
for with gentle and great spirit, though they suffered the utmost torments,
they wished to be the cause of punishment to no one.
Let no harsh sentence of yours make anyone guilty;
do not hasten to punish anyone with stern judgment.
You see the slender splinter in your brother's eye,
and do not know that a beam is in your own eyes.
Unjustly will he wish to describe another's life
who cannot defend his own.
But we, though condemned for our vices, persist in them,
and the very things we attack we soon do ourselves.
Believe it a sin to deceive! The saying stands firm:
'The mouth that lies slays the soul with death.'
Remember always to say what is true,
and let your speech not utter what is not so.
Moreover, put a bridle on your sweet-loving palate,
lest taste rage with its ancient enticements.
Greedy gluttony made those who possessed
the gifts and kingdom of heaven mortal.
For we rush the more into what is forbidden and covet what is denied,
and what is difficult, that we would rather have.
Above all, refuse to flood your veins with lavish wine,
lest wines suddenly become venoms.
As, whenever the dry earth thirsts in excessive heat,
the earth the skilful farmer readies for its crops,
if thick clouds drench the sodden days
before the sun can kill the uprooted weeds,
at once, alas, it will bear in wicked abundance
thorns and grasses harmful to the harvest, the good seed overcome:
so bodies that have been given over to much wine
are lost to good counsel and run riot with vices.
And what will ever be more sordid, what more unsightly,
than for drunkenness to steal you from yourself?
When the head lolls this way and that, the step totters,
the mind refuses its sense and the tongue to hold its sound,
and the drooping eyes close in heavy sleep,
you would not know what you are doing even as you do it.
Why should I speak of the heat brought to a fuming face,
of words let loose in ill-ordered measures,
of cups slipping from hands, and of food mixed with wine
often coming back up over the very tables,
and of you, through countless motions as the wounded mind wills,
now rejoicing too much, now weeping too much,
now whirling your sagging limbs in a dance,
now waving your arms in wanton choruses?
One would like to cry out: buried in wine and feasting,
perhaps forgetting even your own name,
when will the pious care of praying come upon you,
of praying to the God who so generously gives you such things?
How many of the needy could be fed with such great expense,
how many happy days could this one day provide?
But now, while you are full, a hungry pauper wanders before you:
you vomit up wine, while the other scarcely has water.
And if perhaps a needy voice asks for food, you will refuse
to those who have nothing the very thing that you have to spare.
I sense that you have long been saying silently, reader:
'True indeed, but what you lay down is hard.'
Hard things are commanded us; to climb from earth to heaven
is not something you should think can be done with little labour.
Great indeed is the labour, but great is the reward of the labour.
Let him who hopes for prizes flee from sloth.
No one will carry off the palm unless he has first contended;
the sweet crown is given only to the victor.
Or if you were seeking the fragile honours of the world,
by what service would you hope to win a man's favour?
Whatever it is that troubles bodies with various cruelties
while we run through life in the swift racecourse:
contempt, rain, cold, fasting, quarrels,
you could bear them all with patient mind;
running about to make the rounds of the city all day long,
scarcely returning home exhausted in the middle of the night,
and at once rising again at first light
so as to be the first to approach the closed doors.
And when a light sleep has forced you, weary,
to lay down your head on the hard benches,
perhaps the one who arrived later will go in first,
and your foolish complaint will be dinned into your acquaintances' ears.
Or if your voice, raised too loud, reaches the lictor,
pray that you may go away merely pushed aside and not badly beaten.
But suppose, what is rare, that the doorkeeper, won over by gold
and by entreaties, at last says, 'You may go in.'
You enter, coaxing in speech and modest in face,
submissive in bearing: yet these things help not at all.
Every honour has its price: you will advance by the weight of your coin,
whether you seek it by charter, by letters, or by tablets.
For if the rich hand stops giving, the business comes to nothing,
and if you give only words, you too will get only words.
Lo, office has smiled on you, which by custom, in due order,
one takes up late indeed, but lays down quickly.
For what you had given, soon another and another will pay:
what many desire, no one has held for long.
Yet suppose the office lasts long, puffs you up and drives you on:
will it, then, never come to an end?
Come, imagine that the lasting Fasti record your name,
and a happy year passes under your title:
what use, in the end, is power when it ceases to be?
In what can one feel that it was, and is gone?
The age that gradually follows will not know of it,
and even if it knew, what reward would that be to you?
But you who spend yourself so wholly on earthly honour,
who now court men with such ambition:
if you would please Christ the Lord, to whom all things belong,
and win besides the kingdom of God,
you will gain the true in place of the false, the vast in place of the small,
the magnificent in place of the cheap, the everlasting in place of the lost.
What wrong, after all, will overcome a devoted heart?
Will anything be too lofty? What is difficult for you?
For nothing is hard when hope follows on, and all labour,
overcome by honour, comes to fruit,
and to fruit that lasts for all time, which
no prodigal, impatient office-seeker can take away.
You hear the Lord promising new rewards to the just,
who will always give better things than he has promised,
things not seen by the eyes, not whispered into the ears,
not even imagined beforehand by the mind itself.
Now for you the myrrh trees drip from their precious bark,
the earth swells with fragrant turf of incense.
Add thyme, violets, cassia, melilot and saffron;
join white lilies to crimson roses.
If, a sinner, you receive so many gifts in these lands,
what good things will you receive in heaven as a saint?
Come, imagine whatever is bright, whatever beautiful, whatever precious,
whatever you think great in all the world,
as being given to the blessed for their merits: golden roofs,
jewelled doorposts and floors of purple,
and countryside ever fragrant with springtime flowers,
and rivers flowing full of milk and honey together.
Because these things rise up in our minds and are seen by the mind,
believe that they are inferior to those good things to come.
Yet do not fear that, worn down by a long time,
you will be found unequal to God's commands.
This brief life that we now enjoy has nothing long in it,
though it is driven round in a long revolution.
All things, weary, look toward their aging end,
and already the hour is rolling on into the last day.
See how swiftly death has crushed the whole world,
how many peoples the violence of war has struck down.
Not thick forests, not the rough slopes of a lofty mountain,
not rivers strong with rushing whirlpools,
not fortresses by their sites, not cities safe within their walls,
not the pathless sea, not the grim desert,
not hollows, not even caves under gloomy cliffs
could succeed in eluding barbarian hands.
For many, feigned good faith, for many, perjury,
for many, betrayal by fellow citizens was the cause of death.
Ambush did much, open violence did much.
What was not overcome by force was overcome by famine.
The unhappy mother fell with her children and her husband;
the master underwent slavery together with his slaves.
Some lay as food for dogs; for many their burning houses,
which snatched away their lives, provided a pyre.
Through villages and estates, through fields and crossroads and all
the districts, on every road this way and that,
were death, grief, destruction, burning, mourning.
All Gaul smoked on a single pyre.
Yet why should I list the deaths of a crumbling world,
which always take place along their accustomed course?
Why should I recount how many die throughout the world,
when you yourself may see your own day hastening on?
I pass over how much is allowed to the sword, how much to ruins,
to fire, to hail, to floods;
how many war, famine and raging diseases destroy,
and the one death that rushes in by various ways;
and how many, even in time of peace, so that there may
be peace, the due penalty tortures as guilty [?].
Every hour, little by little, brings us nearer to death:
even in this time while we speak, we are dying beforehand.
And along its deceptive course, with silent effort,
the last of life presses on toward the final days.
While food and sleep, while words and cups soothe us,
whether you sit at home or travel to foreign lands,
and whatever you do or do not do, death of its own accord
moves its feet in turn, never delaying.
As a wax candle, set out in the time of blind night
to make up for the day by the service of its light,
is consumed by a slow fire while we do not notice,
and the devouring flame always hastens to the end:
so it is with the affairs of men: whatever is done perishes,
and what life draws out for itself advances and dies.
But suppose such long spans of vigorous old age
that, yourself untouched, you look on the deaths of the world:
though it come late, yet that end must come
which cannot be altogether absent.
For things that are born grow, and afterwards grow old,
and for those worn out by age nothing remains but death.
He who has lived thirty years [?]
and he who has lived [?] a thousand,
once the final end has taken hold of both,
are surely the same at the last moment of death.
What good is it to have drawn out life, if you cease to live?
Or what reward is there in good things, if you are held fast by evils,
since you are touched by the fruit of enjoyment only while you enjoy it [?],
and this life lives in the service of life [?]?
For what has been is nothing if it ceases to be,
and what you do not feel, it does not help you that it was.
What use, then, if fasting troubles you,
is it to have loaded your limbs heavily with yesterday's food,
and, when thirst today constricts your dry throat,
to have been soaked the day before with too much [?]?
For the day that will not return snatches away the feeling
of all that has run its course in that swift revolution.
But we, when the flower of early youth has run its course,
unsteady now in step, sight, voice and hand,
when it is pain to remember all that we once were,
and the most recent things rob all the past of credit,
bent, querulous, our bodies worn out, are never
satisfied enough even with this life, burdensome as it is.
Hence it is that, as though wholly removed from the whole world,
we look on at whatever perishes in all the world.
The death of others warns us wretches of our own,
as though we lived under another sun.
Before our eyes and far away alike we are robbed of friends,
and grief comes to us from there through the eyes, from here through the ear.
Dear parents die as their years decline,
and a wife is snatched from her husband's very lap.
Death takes a brother from his brother's embrace,
and perhaps he was the younger by birth.
Nor is the older age always taken first in the order of life,
when a father sees the cruel funeral of his son.
Yet no one is wary enough to believe what he sees,
and to see that he too may suffer what he does not want.
This, however, comes from the fact that, because our deeds are always wicked,
we think death a perpetual evil,
and the punishments that the holy law threatens for crimes
we count it gain to receive later.
Happy is he who thinks the end of his labours a lawful thing,
who, so as not to fear afterwards, has taken care beforehand by fearing.
Happy is he who, secure in the uprightness of his life,
can look forward with steady mind and calm face
to the great and glorious judgment, to be set in motion
with great inquiry before cities and peoples;
whom a mind well conscious of itself, on sure grounds,
makes able to hold his head unafraid beneath so great a weight.
There those once mighty in empire and kingdom,
there those conspicuous with the fasces and robes of state,
whose custom it was to load gold with choice dishes, crystal with Falernian,
and couches with coverings of purple;
those famed for strength, praised for the gift of beauty,
and wrongly trusting in the body's resources;
whose belly was their master, wantonness their prayer,
their hope in the present, their glory in riches;
who, wretches, neglected to seek the Lord
even at death itself, as their eyes were about to close,
will await punishment, shut in. Do not ask to be told
what punishment: a punishment fitting their deeds awaits them.
Perpetual darkness will hold some in blind night;
for others a fierce flame will then give light [?].
These will be forced, with mangled bodies, to climb
furnaces blazing with sulphurous fire.
Those will be bound by hard ice, poured over them in violent rigour
and frozen by wintry blasts.
And though the nature of Gehenna wars so discordantly,
the force of that single name is yet manifold.
Nor could you tell, in punishments so diverse,
whether torment by fire or by cold is the heavier.
It is not as with us here, where, for those slain by an earthly death,
many crimes receive only one death,
since the judge, however harsh in proportion to the gravity of the deeds,
can do no more than take away the life,
and, by a kind of profit from crime, if many remain,
the first punishment denies vengeance for the rest.
But there a punishment fitted to the deeds will follow
and pay off every offence in its order.
And one body will lie open, limb by limb,
to as many punishments as the vices it was capable of.
One law will punish the cruel, another the greedy;
deeds will pay in one way, intentions in another.
Perjurers have their own punishment, the proud have theirs,
and the shedding of blood will be another charge.
The envious, the impatient, the effeminate, the forger, the adulterer,
he who is wholly given to wine, wholly given to lust,
he whose right hand is guilty of slaughter, whose tongue is quick to abuse,
the usurper, the boaster, the impious, the unteachable,
will pay their penalties before the day of judgment,
so that the delay of judgment gives not even a short respite from torment.
Serpents with sinuous coils will wind about some,
while a chain glowing with fire will chafe others.
All there is full of tears, terror and pain,
and there is no voice but what groaning utters.
Why should I run on further through each separate crime
and the dire torments that will rack the wretched?
For even now, if you say anything with a careless mouth,
you must give an account of that speech.
Among these, whoever has denied the Lord of all things,
bowing his head to stones and stocks of wood,
he will be truly wretched, yet pitied by no one.
He alone will receive whatever does harm anywhere.
Countless worms will live in his dying body,
and there will be no end to the smoke the fire gives off.
But on the other side the gentle and pious [?],
if, when wronged, they did not repay evil,
but gave help to the wretched, food to the one who asked,
affection to their acquaintances, service to their fathers,
will shine with eyes like the blazing sun,
their splendid limbs clothed in snow-white robes.
And especially those whom the nights receive and the days find
ready in the law of Christ,
whose vow it was never to stain the snow-white garment of baptism
in the beds of women,
chaste not in body alone but in all their heart,
such as I would wish you, my reader, to be;
or those already blessed, which is the highest glory, who, having conquered
the enticements of the light and of the faithless body,
and seeking the true life, did not fear
to pour out their devoted souls for the name of Christ.
This company of saints will also include priests
and monks set apart from the whirlwinds of men,
who now, spurning the delights of flattering fame,
hope for the rewards of the coming judgment.
Leading a gentle leisure, their affairs secure,
they live well now by their merit, and better hereafter.
For they will throng about the King in dense array,
when the Lord stands upon the earth as judge,
and wherever the Lamb turns, they will all go,
bathed in the true light, the light of God.
And their quickened faces will take on such splendour
that they cannot be looked upon by the eyes of those who see them.
So, when the hollow trumpet has sounded its terrible call,
bearing witness at last to the coming of God,
soon the earth will lie open, torn by long fissures,
and flames, lightning and hail will rush down everywhere,
the world shaken to its deepest foundations,
while every road this way and that is in ferment.
Here sad groans, there the holy joys of life:
one voice in the different companies.
And every father will go hastily with quickened step,
leading his children and his lineage,
and every line will be drawn along in one continuous train,
the ancestor in the midst of his descendants.
I will not speak to you of famous cities and distant nations
and kingdoms that are now or have been,
of peoples not made sluggish by cold or scorched by the sun,
those whom the rising and the setting day have held;
but whatever was born from the time of the first world
until the day that will be the world's end,
the first command will gather the souls, just and guilty,
from all lands into one place.
Yet not one among so many thousands will go there
who has not been counted by its Lord.
Soon, mounting the glowing tribunal in that same flesh
which he had borne into heaven, glorifying man,
all things that slip by in order through the remaining ages,
what [happens] then and what thereafter, the law abiding [?],
he, holy of countenance, lofty on his throne, terrible to see,
conspicuous yet scarcely to be looked upon, will judge.
And amid trails of flame and the sounds of trumpets,
amid angelic choirs and the holy army,
amid the pallor, weeping, joys, prayers and fears
of infants and mothers, of the young and the old,
the final sentence will be given to the waiting throng,
sounding from the mouth of the most holy Judge:
'Go into rest and praise, company of the just,
never to be parted from my kingdom,
which the Father, knowing your merit and the life to come,
gives you now, a gift prepared long ago.
But you, crowd ever opposed to my commands,
impious, be shut up in the places of hell.'
There teeth will gnash and eyes will weep,
to be tormented by boundless fires.
And so that whatever is commanded may truly endure,
this will be the decree of the eternal judgment:
glory, with death removed, will hold the just,
and the guilty will not die, so as to bear punishment.
These things, reader, I ought to have taught you by deeds,
so that a life of proven worth might give weight to my words.
But since we wretches neglect whatever we are advised,
and it is easier to learn than to do,
if you commit to your mind all that has come in through your ear,
all that has been set out in my writings,
I will say with confidence: received into heaven's dwelling,
you will shake off the hard chains of cruel death.
And you who were before a son of Gehenna
will begin to be a son of God most high.
To these one thing remains, without which all else profits nothing:
that you believe Christ is from the Father and with the Father,
and that, the Holy Spirit being joined without distinction,
the three names make up one God.
But you, whoever reads my little book,
whether he is bad or good, remember me.
And as often as, having read the poem through,
you pray to Christ the Lord, let me always be on your lips.
Do not believe that I ask this only with the edge of my lips,
or think that you may safely ignore it:
so may no day pierce you with bitter cares,
so may all that you do please Christ,
so may you receive a holy crown from the Lord's hand,
let not the remembrance of my name leave you,
so that I, Orientius, who surpass all sinners,
may win pardon through the prayers of the saints.
